Passed February 2, 1820. From the Connecticut Gazette. I would advise every farmer not to be too ambitious of a numerous herd of cattle, or stock of sheep; nor to keep more of either than he can keep in a thriving state. If he owns two pair of steers, or two yoke of oxen, and cannot keep their furies loose and hair slick, he must sell one. If he has ten cows, and makes small cheese, let him sell two; if that does not enlarge his cheese, let him sell two more. If his sheep be feeble, and cast their wool, let him examine his flock; if it consists of fifty, let him immediately sell ten at least. From his flock let him annually select the oldest, and the weakest of the young, and either sell them at a fair price, or feed them himself for market. With us, sheep of more than thirty in a flock, seldom answer well. Of breeds of sheep I say nothing.

State Agricultural Society,' was announced by them on Friday at the State Fair at Utica. The highest prize for the best mower, and the second prize as a reaper, was awarded to J. H. Manny, of Illinois. There were twelve different machines in competition, among which were the celebrated McCormick's & Hussey's reapers. Manny's seems to have some important advantages over all the others, which consist in the perfection of the cutting apparatus, and its adjustability to various heights of cutting, and also a very important advantage seems to exist in the peculiar combination of a reaping and mowing machine, by which it is equally well adapted to both purposes; the placing in, or removing a loose platform, being the only change necessary to convert it from one to another. These two awards must, in our judgment, place Manny's machine at the head of mowers and reapers on the present trial. The combination must be especially valuable to farmers who require a machine both for reaping and mowing, and we regard it as a great triumph that the best mowing machine is awarded to be the second best reaper, beating McCormick's & Hussey's, of world renowned celebrity. Editor News: Your paper comes to us enriched with an article from the pen of Miss Gardiner, "The Education of the Heart," and we cannot forbear speaking a word in praise and admiration of so worthy a production. Miss G. came to your county a stranger, only a year since, and has been commendably unselfish, in that she has entered the field of moral and intellectual improvement with her whole heart and head. We like the tenor of her essay very much, and are sure that the Gregory Association need be proud of her cooperation.

The Southern Press. Vol. 1. Washington, Monday, September 3, 1850. No. 66. AGRICULTURAL ASSOCIATION. THE Fifth Annual fair of the Southern Central Agricultural Association, will be held during the week embracing Wednesday, the 14th day of August next, which is the day of the fifth annual meeting at Atlanta, Georgia. The Committee charged with the duty of prescribing such general rules as they may deem necessary to a proper management of the approaching Fair, have adopted the following General Regulations. 1st The Fair Grounds and Buildings will be opened for visitors on Monday morning, and continue open until Friday evening. It is therefore desirable that all persons having articles for exhibition, shall be on the ground as early as Friday or Saturday, the 9th and 10th August when a Committee will be there ready to receive them.

To our surprise, but one sample of coffee is presented this year, that of Mr. B. Pitman, of Hilo. It is of excellent quality, and takes the premium. Wheat. There is no competitor for the first premium in wheat, but we are of opinion that H. J. G. Croswell of East Maui, is entitled to the second prize, which we award him accordingly. Several fair samples of wheat in the ear are presented. Corn. We award the first premium in corn, to the Rev. J. S. Emerson of Waialua, and the second to Lieut Reynolds, of Kauai. The corn exhibited by Mr. Emerson is very fine, and we take pleasure in noticing several samples of fair quality, from other parties. Oats. No competitor for the prize. A fair specimen of oats in the ear is exhibited by John Smith, of East Maui. Barley. We award the premium for Barley to Mr. Hollingsworth, of Ewa, who presents samples of two different kinds. Specimens of Barley in the ear are exhibited from Maui. Arrow-root. There are three competitors for this prize, and the specimens exhibited are all choice. We award the premium to the Rev. C. B. A CATTLE SHOW and FAIR will be held at James Bishop's in Watertown, on Tuesday the first of October next, for the purpose of buying and selling Cattle, or swapping and matching Oxen and Steers. There will also be offered for sale Working Oxen, Beef and Store Cattle, Young Cattle, Calves, etc. It is desired by subscribers of all those who may have gunteined or odd Steers, to get them together for the purpose of matching them. It is time and trouble of one day to get together to match their as match cattle always sell higher and quicker than others. All those who may have two years old Cattle, or Yearlings, or Calves, please bring them on. There will also be at the Fair four Bakewell Bucks, two of which are lambs, lately purchased by the subscriber, of Thomas Dunn, Esq. of Albany county, N. Y. which he thinks will be worth the attention of the farmers generally. Should the weather be stormy or unpleasant on Tuesday the 1st, it will continue the next day after. GEORGE MERCHANT. The wide circulation we have obtained assures us that the Farmer already meets the wants of the agricultural community and encourages us to renewed exertions to make it fully deserving of the patronage awarded it. The New England Farmer is published weekly, in folio form. One entire page is occupied exclusively with articles relating to agriculture, nearly all original, and written for our columns by men of practical experience on their own farms. Our leading object is to give the results of practical operations and the knowledge drawn from them and not mere speculations or plausible theories. The remainder of the paper contains: A carefully prepared digest of the News of the Week, as full and accurate as constant care can make it. Miscellaneous Reading for the family circle, always instructive and of good moral tone, as well as entertaining. Market Reports and Prices Current, including the best and only reliable report of the Cambridge and Brighton Cattle Markets, prepared exclusively for our columns at great expense.
